         Transcript of the Statement of the Prime Minister of Barbados


              The Honourable Mia Amor Mottley, S.C., M.P.,





                     On the Occasion of the



     GENERAL DEBATE OF THE, 77™SESSION OF THE UNITED NATIONS

                      GENERAL ASSEMBLY



                                  At




              THE UNITED NATIONS GENERAL ASSEMBLY





                       Thursday, September 22, 2022





     UNITED NATIONS HEADQUARTES, NEW YORK                                please check against delivery

Thank you very much Mr. President.

  ! would like, first of all, to congratulate you on your election to this Honourable Assembly as its
 president and as    | do so,      | want to at the outset express my appreciation for the courageous
 leadership and commitment in very difficult times of our Secretary-General, Antonio Guterres,
 and the Deputy Secretary-General, Amina Mohammed.


 This year, we come again and the battles continue. Indeed, they have been intensified with what
we have seen over the course of the summer and what we have seen over the course of this year;
 with the war in Ukraine and the concomitant consequences to ordinary people all over the globe;
 with respect to inflation; with respect to scarcity of supply of goods; with respect simply to
 hardship. Challenges  in accessing food, continue  regrettably, to be a  characteristic of the
environment within which we live.


  | had hoped that we would have seen improvement, but   | am now convinced more than ever that
there comes atime when we must heed a certain call, as was said when others before us - when
  | was a student - sought to fight the great famine in Africa and came together as one world to
make that defining difference.

Last year    | asked us to do the same. And maybe it is, in the wordsofJimmy Cliff, that we have to
keep trying and trying and trying. But the world must stand up  if our citizens are to live a better
 life.        | say so today, because  it is easy to come here only and complain. But the truth is that  it is
within our power to make that difference and that defining change.

We must decide whether we want to stand for peace and whether we want to stand for love and
whether we want to stand for prosperity - knowing that we choose to do so at the most difficult
time and from the most difficult and dark place that we have done so in a very, very long time.


 | believe it is possible.


But  it is up to us to change possibilities into realities. What do               | mean?

Mr. President, we have been speaking for a long time about the reform of this institution and
about the fact that only about a quarter of today’s membership was  in existence when this
institution was formed.



Earlier this week, President Biden spoke of the need to reform the Security Council. We call and
echo that. But we go further because we believe that a Security Council, where the power of the
veto remains in the hands of a few, will still lead us to war, as we have seen this year. Therefore,
the reform must not simply be in its composition, but also see the abolition of that veto.





                                                                                                           1

We also believe that the G7 and the G20 must be more inclusive. We have been calling year after
 year for the inclusion of representation of the people of Africa and African in the G7 and G20. For
 how can a world have at its core a subcommittee that excludes more than 1.4 billion people and
 expect  it to reflect fairness and transparency in its decision-making?


 If we are to move from possibilities to realities, we must embrace a transparent framework that
 allows our people, who are losing faith in their institutions and in the governance of this world,
 to understand that fairness means something; that fairness means the ability for all to have a
 voice. We can't only speak to it within the corridors of democracy, within the nation state, but  it
 will only mean something when  it also  is reflected  in our international community. And  if  |,
 perhaps, have one simple theme today,  it  is that that fairness and that togetherness  is what is
needed to bring about peace, love and prosperity in this world.


And no, this is not romanticism. These are hard realities that simply require decisions. And that
 is why   | use that language from that great anthem, "We Are the World".


There comes a time when we must heed a certain call that the world must come together as one.
 Regrettably, there are too many people dying in conflicts. We must make decisions to reform and
to fight for peace, not to fight to sustain war - wherever it is found across this world - to fight for
reform so that our citizens are not made victims of poverty because of the triple crisis of climate,
of pandemic and indeed now of the conflict that is causing the inflationary pressures that lead,
regrettably, to people taking matters into their own hands, as we have seen in Haiti in the last

week,


Any attempt to increase fuel prices, in any part of the world, by 150% would have been met with
great consternation and anger by populations on fixed income. And when that happens in one of
the poorest countries in the world that has been trying for almost 230 years to find stability,
against the backdrop of exploitation that it has faced, we ask ourselves: when will the world stand
up and be counted for the people of Haiti?


Similarly, we ask for the same transparency to occur with respect to the removal of the blockade
against the people of Cuba. This is the 30th year that a UN resolution has called for the removal
of that blockade, but the blockade has been there for 60 years. And    | say simply to the people of
the United States of America, do not be short-sighted in your goals, For in this hemisphere, peace
and prosperity is a province of all.





Yes, there may be problems on both sides, but there is nothing that justifies further hardship to
people because of ideological differences. And  if there are human  rights differences,  let us
resolve them, as we have chosen to do with mightier countries across the world without the
imposition of sanctions.



                                                                                                           2

Fairness and transparency demand  it of us.

 But  | also want to talk to you about other solutions that we believe can alter our condition without
 imposing unreasonable burdens of taxation on the populations of the world.


We live in a world, as   | said last year, where the disparity in income is too great. And we live in a
world where some are even benefiting from the crises, disproportionately and egregiously. And
we must ask ourselves, therefore, whether the time has not come for a review of the settlement
 of the Bretton Woods institutions that no longer serve the purpose in the 21st century that they
served in the 20th century; the purpose that they served when they were catering to a quarter
 of the nation states that are now members of this august institution.


We ask ourselves whether the time has not come for our voices to act collectively, to demand
action through the boards of directors of those institutions. And why do   | say so?


The International Bank for Reconstruction and Development  is really what the World Bank  is
 called. And maybe  if we referred to that continuously, we would remind ourselves that the
purpose of reconstruction and development must be appropriate to the century in which we live.
And the century in which we live does not only demand of us the eradication of poverty, which
remains a noble goal, but it demands of us, equally, the protection of global public goods.


All of us here know what  it is like to be on the frontlines of the public health crisis. All of us here,
now know what it is to be on the frontline of the climate crisis.


Years ago, we spoke about Small Island Developing States being on the front line because we
were the canaries in the coal mine. Today we speak of all countries. And this hot, hot summer -
with wildfires in California; heat waves in North America and Europe; the drying up of waterways
in Europe; the floods in China and the apocalyptic floods in Pakistan. Our heart goes out to the
people of those and all other countries which have suffered.


This simply cannot continue.


And any attempt to deny that the climate crisis has manmade origins  is an attempt to delude
ourselves and to admit that we want to be accomplices  in the continued death and loss and
damage that ensues to the people who are the victims of it. Our people demand better of us.



We believe, today, that the most appropriate place to deal with global public goods  is, in fact,
the World Bank Group.   | simply want to say that companies, multinational companies that have
contributed to or benefited from global public risk should contribute to creating global public
goods. They should do this through a percentage, a small percentage oftheir profits, funding the
needs of countries - whether it is on the issue of climate; stability and resilience and adaptation;
whether it is for the protection of biodiversity both on land and in our waters; whether  it  is for




                                                                                           3

the protection of public health against the next pandemic  , including the slow motion pandemic
 of antimicrobial resistance or others that we have not even contemplated; or the provision of
 education for each of our citizens. Because to remain on this earth without the benefit of

 education is to be sentenced to life imprisonment from a young age; or access to electricity which
 600  million people  in Africa do without; or the equivalent to the  right to knowledge and
 prosperity in our age, that is access to broadband; and of course, as   | said to the United States
 Congress last week, the right to a bank account, because countries across the world are being
 denied the right to access correspondent banking, jeaving their citizens and their economies to
 function as financial pariahs in a world that  is supposed to be globally interdependent for the
 movement of capital.


 My friends,


The provision of that fund to promote public goods at a global level is critical if we are to make a
 difference going forward, and to achieve the peace, the love and the prosperity to which     |
 referred.


   | want to commend the International Monetary Fund for the rapid financing mechanism they
 deployed at the beginning of the pandemic; and, for the Resilience and Sustainability Trust (RST)
that is about to be launched. This  is a first recognition that middle income countries should be
 able to access funding irrespective of per capita income, but dependent on climate vulnerability.
And we say, do not simply make  it available to countries following a disaster, but let us do it for
countries before the disaster - for every dollar spent before saves $7 in avoided expenditure, not
to mention the lives that are saved.


We don't want only to pay the undertaker, we want to save lives.


But   | ask the IMF to reflect on the fact that the Resilience and Sustainability Trust may need to
be delinked from quotas  if  it  is to be effective.     | am conscious that that will depend on more
countries seeding that fund with capital and more countries agreeing perhaps to allow their
Special Drawing Rights (SDRs) to be used there; just as we asked them to allow those Special
Drawing Rights to be used to allow multilateral development banks to significantly increase the
money that  is available to countries, particularly at this time, as we are on the verge of a debt
crisis where more than 45 countries are facing the heat of the moment because of the increased
cost of capital, as a result of the monetary policies that are being put in place to fight the virulent
cancer of inflation.


 | say now that we want to thank those countries that have come together to help us continue the
financing of Sustainable Development Goals. And we link this to the global public goods. Why?
Because they're fundamentally, the right to development. They are fundamentally the right to
give each person the ability to live a good life. And we can't be lost in the conflict and lost in the
climate crisis and lost in the pandemic, and forget fundamentally what our mission  is.


| commend those who continue to remember that.




                                                                                4

But    | ask for us to reach a global compact; financing for development cannot be built on short-
 term financing;  it must be spread over at least 30 years. The world recognised that when  it
 allowed Britain the refinance of its World War   | bonds which were only paid off eight years ago,
 100 years after World War One started.


 Or when  it allowed Germany to cap  its debt service at the equivalent of 3% of  its exports,
 conscious that the cataclysmic experience of war would not have allowed them to finance
 reconstruction while repaying debts incurred for war.


My friends, we are no different today.


We have incurred debts to deal with COVID-19. We have incurred debts to fight the climate crisis.
And we have incurred debts, now, to fight this difficult moment with the inflationary crisis and
 with the absence of certainty of supply of goods. Why, therefore, must the developing world now
 seek to find funding over 7 to 10 years when others had the benefit of longer periods to repay
 their debt?


 In Barbados, we had the good fortune to gather a large number of persons from civil society and
 in academia at the end of July of this year. And we settled on what we have come to call the
 Bridgetown Agenda.   It  is to be  a Bridgetown Agenda for peace, a Bridgetown Agenda for
 prosperity, a Bridgetown Agenda inspired by love of humanity. And  it is that agenda that speaks
to the reform of the Bretton Woods architecture.


We've asked and will ask countries and people to join  it because we believe that unless we take
responsibility for ourselves, unless we accept that we are the world, we're not going to see a
change. And as   | come to this issue of climate, which will dominate the next 45 days as we go to
Egypt, let us remember that the trust that is needed to propel us to fight the great causes of our
time will not be won by us breaching promises.


The developing world, and in particular the Small island Developing States went to Paris in 2015
and agreed to a global compact. One of the key aspects of it that allowed us to do so, was the
promise of addressing the issue of loss and damage.




Today, the people of Guadeloupe and Puerto Rico. Yesterday, Turks and Caicos. And little do we
know what will happen with Bermuda — facing the disruption of Hurricane Fiona.


This morning,     | received news about difficulties for natural gas supply in my own country.      |
suspect others  in  this  part of the world face  similar issues because  of the  facilities, the
installations that have been affected in Puerto Rico. This comes at a time when access to that

commodity has already been affected by the war in Ukraine and the decision by Russia to cease
supply to Europe.




                                                                                           5

When we match this with the reality that we have not planned in detail how we will create the
 capacity to meet the commitments that we have made for net zero  - and I'm a big defender of
 net zero - as you know, then    | see trouble ahead of us. We must pause and get it right.


 Our small states are making commitments that the world wants to hear, but when those
 commitments are undermined by an inability to supply the electric cars or the batteries necessary
 to sustain renewable energy, then we know we have a problem.


And   | ask us, today, to recognise that those commitments on loss and damage and that matching
 of commitment to capacity, are absolutely critical  if we are to make serious progress in saving
 our world.


  | want to salute Denmark for its commitment on Tuesday to be able to propose $13 million US
 dollars to a loss and damage fund, for it represents the first acknowledgment by a North Atlantic
 country that there is a justifiable need and justice in the demand for this loss and damage claim.



My friends,


 If we don't speak truth to our population and if we don't explain and have mature conversations,
 rather than to rely on the headlines and the soundbites, we will find a disconnect between those
who are governed and those who are governing. And therefore,  let us to the task, move with
 dispatch, not for soundbites, but for difficult conversations, to secure the peace of this world, to
secure the prosperity of our people, and to underpin  it with a love for humanity, which was the
original purpose of this organization.

 In the words of that song, again, "Let us lend a hand to life, for it is the greatest gift of all. And we
can't pretend day by day, that someone somewhere else is going to make that change. This is our
family. This is our world. And this is our time to make that defining difference."


Many of the things that  I've put before us today, don't require money, but they require a
commitment and they require political  will. And with the power of the pen, we can impose
natural disaster and pandemic clauses in our debt. With the power of the pen, we can change
the capital that is available to multilateral development banks that will remove the barriers that
currently exists for us to fight poverty.


With those commitments, we can make a difference  in today's world. And  let us do  so,
recognizing  that  a world  that  reflects  an  imperialistic  order and  hypocrisy and  lack  of
transparency will not achieve that mission. But one that gives us freedom, transparency and a
level playing field can make that definable difference.


Thank you very much,
